questions.q: Per this lesson, where does Salesforce-specific technical debt show up most, beyond old Apex code?
options: It never appears outside of Apex code on Salesforce
Only in orgs that have never been upgraded to a new seasonal release
Only in the physical data center hosting the org
Declarative sprawl -- duplicate automations, unexplained fields, layered permission sets, and unused reports consuming ongoing maintenance attention
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that Salesforce technical debt shows up heavily in declarative sprawl -- fields, automations, and permission sets accumulated over time -- not primarily in code.

questions.q: What does Security Health Check do, as described in this lesson?
options: It automatically deletes unused fields from an org
It replaces the need for a Change Advisory Board
It scores an org's security settings against Salesforce's recommended baseline and flags specific configuration gaps
It tracks how often each seasonal release is adopted
questions.explain: Security Health Check is a real Setup tool that measures an org's security configuration against Salesforce's recommended baseline, giving a direct, measurable view into one slice of org health.

questions.q: What practical problem does this lesson say dedicating a fixed percentage of release capacity to debt reduction is meant to solve?
options: That cleanup work competes with new feature work for the same limited release capacity, and new feature work almost always wins that argument without a protected allocation
That technical debt is usually completely unknown to the organization
That Salesforce charges extra for orgs with high technical debt
That debt reduction work is illegal without a dedicated budget line
questions.explain: The lesson identifies the real failure mode as competition for limited release capacity -- protecting a fixed percentage for cleanup keeps it from losing out feature-by-feature to new work.

questions.q: What is a data dictionary, per this lesson?
options: A list of every Salesforce API method available to developers
A living record of what each field, object, and major automation is for, who owns it, and why it exists
A Salesforce Setup page that tracks login history
A tool that automatically writes Apex test classes
questions.explain: A data dictionary records ownership and purpose for fields, objects, and automations, making it fast for the next person to check whether something can be safely removed instead of requiring archaeology.

questions.q: Before deleting a suspicious-looking, seemingly unused field, what does this lesson recommend as a cheap first-pass check?
options: Deleting it immediately without any investigation, since unused fields carry no risk
Asking Salesforce Support to make the deletion decision
Waiting exactly one full seasonal release cycle with no other action
Checking the Setup Audit Trail and field history data to confirm whether it's actually still being touched before committing to deeper analysis
questions.explain: The lesson recommends using Setup Audit Trail and field history as a cheap first check on whether a field or automation is genuinely unused, before investing in deeper investigation or removal.
